Second War of the Diadochi

The death of Antipater sees the unpopular Polyperchon assume his place instead of Antipater's son, Cassander. Feeling owed the regency as his father's heir, Cassander sought allies among the diadochi to see himself to position. Thus begins the Second War of the Diadochi.

Strategos Polyperchon

Before Antipater passed, he declared Polyperchon to succeed him as regent for Alexander's empire. This decision deeply aggrieved the late Antipater's son and heir, Cassander, and he sought alliances among the other Diadochi. This disagreement soon erupted into the 2nd Diadochi war.
Satrapes Eumenes

Secretary to the late Alexander, Eumenes has since made a name for himself as a quality commander at the battle of the Hellespont, where he killed the much praised Krateros only to accept subservience to Antigonus at the close of the 1st war. Now that the Diadochi have again geared up to war, he breaks with Antigonus and throws lots with the new Regent.
Strategos Kassandros

His father, Antipater, recently passed, however rather naming him, as his lawful son and heir, Antipater passed over Kassander in favor of his friend Polyperchon. This slight against Kassander sends him to seek alliance among the other Diadochi and soon the Empire ignites into war once again.
Satrapes Antigonos "Monophthalmos"

Securing himself as master of Asia following the 1st War, the death of Antipater and his passing over of Kassander, Antigonus sees new opportunity to expand with the the later's appeal for support. Soon the Diadochi divide sides between the Regent and the Claimant. The Second War of the Diadochi will soon begin.
Satrapes Ptolemaios

One of Alexander's chief commanders, Ptolemy has shown crafty amibition since the late King's death. Securing himself in Egypt and even seizing the king's body, enterring it in his province. Now that the Diadochi march to war once again over the Regency, the Ptolemains have ample oppurtunity to expand their power and influence.
The Rise of Macedon
The Rise of Macedon

Macedon stands on the edge. King Perdiccas III has fallen in battle against the Illyrians, and his brother Philip II takes a shattered throne. Claimants linger, neighboring tribes test the frontier, and Athens backs rivals from afar. Across Greece, old powers guard shrinking influence while petty wars and bruised pride keep the poleis divided. In Sicily, Syracuse wrestles with unrest and watches Carthage with suspicion. In Egypt, Nectanebo II rules a wealthy land but knows Persia has not forgotten its loss. In southern Italy, Tarentum argues with nearby Greek cities and braces against the pressure of Messapian and Lucanian tribes. No single power leads the Mediterranean. Every border looks soft. New players can rise fast, and old names can fall quietly. The future is not promised to anyone. The board is wide open, and the first move belongs to the bold.
King Philip II of Macedon

Philip has just taken control of a collapsing Macedon. Illyrians have killed his brother and press the borders, Paeonian raids cut into the north, and rival claimants still linger. The army is weak and the treasury is thin, but Philip brings hard-earned lessons from Thebes and is already drilling a new pike infantry. If he can hold off hostile tribes and keep Greek cities like Athens from backing his enemies, he can unify Macedon, bend Greece to his will, and set his sights on Persia. One failure ends his rise, but success reshapes everything.
Pharaoh Nectanebo II

Nectanebo II rules Egypt under constant pressure. Persia wants the Nile back and funds rebels and Greek mercenaries against him. Egyptian nobles doubt his strength, and cities in the Delta can turn if Persian gold flows. His power rests on foreign troops and a careful balance of alliances with Greek commanders. At this moment, Persia is preparing another invasion. If he can hold the frontier forts, keep mercenaries loyal, and stop Persian agents inside Egypt, he preserves independence. If he fails, Egypt becomes a satrapy again and his dynasty ends.
King Bardylis I of Illyria

Bardylis is an aging but dangerous warlord whose rise was built on talent, not noble birth. He has bloodied Macedon repeatedly and killed a king in battle, but his power rests on loose tribal loyalty and constant success. Now Macedon has a new ruler, and Philip is reorganizing his army to strike back. Bardylis must cow rival Illyrian chieftains, keep tribute flowing, and beat Macedon before its reforms mature. If he hesitates, his coalition splinters. If he wins, he dominates the Balkans and keeps Greek gold flowing north. His time is limited, but so is his rival’s strength.
Dionysioss II Tyrant of Syracuse

Dionysios II sits on his father’s throne with shaky authority. Syracuse is wealthy and feared, but rival Greek cities in Sicily resent his rule, Carthage watches for weakness, and his own court is a nest of scheming advisers. He relies on mercenaries to keep order, yet their loyalty depends on pay. Philosophers urge reform while generals demand war. If he projects strength, he can keep Carthage at bay and hold the fractious Sicilian cities in line. If he missteps, rebellion and foreign invasion follow.
King Cotys I of the Odrysians

Cotys I rules the Odrysians through fear, gold, and careful bargains with Greek cities along the coast. Thracian nobles are restless and expect spoils, while Athens schemes to keep him from controlling the grain routes. His power depends on bribery, hostage-taking, and punishing rivals before they can unite. Macedon has a new king, and Cotys can either profit from the chaos or face a rising army to the west. One sharp campaign could give him the coastal cities he covets

column2: Archytas of Taras

Archytas leads Taras at its height, a rare mix of statesman, general, and mathematician. His city dominates southern Italy’s Greek colonies, but rising Italic tribes and jealous neighbors test its strength. He depends on swift diplomacy, mercenary skill, and a navy that keeps Taras rich through trade. If he balances local rivals and keeps Lucanian pressure in check, Taras can shape Magna Graecia for a generation. A miscalculation invites tribal raids, political unrest at home, and the slow decline of Tarentine influence. His intellect is unmatched, but the peninsula answers to iron, not theory.
